strengths: LoRWeB addresses a relevant computer-vision problem: transferring visually demonstrated edits to new images. Jointly learning LoRA factors and an input-conditioned, layer-specific router provides a practical adaptation mechanism without per-example optimization.

The same-backbone rank-128 LoRA baseline is a valuable control. LoRWeB achieves 57.9% pairwise VLM preference and 57.6% human preference against it, providing evidence of an improvement beyond simply adopting Flux.1-Kontext.

Evaluation combines perceptual metrics, VLM judgments, human preferences, and qualitative comparisons across 840 triplets and 100 tasks. Aggregating metrics by task helps avoid domination by tasks with more examples.

Figure 7 provides convincing qualitative evidence that reference images influence details beyond the text prompt, including poster lettering and crystal-crown colors. The visual comparisons also illustrate useful improvements in edit fidelity and content preservation.

The supplement reports optimization settings, encoder checkpoints, evaluation prompts, and sources for the community adapters and photographs. Capacity, encoder, input-layout, and normalization ablations provide useful implementation evidence.
weaknesses: The central explanation—that a dynamically composed basis overcomes a single adapter's generalization bottleneck—is not sufficiently isolated. Equation (2) mixes A and B separately, producing a rank-at-most-4 update with cross terms, rather than a linear mixture of adapter updates. The rank-128 baseline approximately matches factor parameters but changes effective rank and conditioning simultaneously. A static rank-4 baseline and fixed-routing ablation would help establish whether dynamic composition, low-rank regularization, or additional conditioning drives the gain. Differentiation from the cited mixture-of-LoRA methods also remains limited.

The strongest generalization claims rely predominantly on a custom benchmark generated using the same Kontext model family as LoRWeB. In-domain prompts are explicitly filtered for successful Kontext edits, while out-of-domain references use Kontext community adapters. This is a useful controlled setting, but potentially favors compatibility with that backbone. Separate results for the public Relation252k tasks, custom in-domain tasks, and custom out-of-domain tasks are needed to assess the claimed breadth of generalization; novel prompt wording alone does not establish semantic task novelty.

The improvement over the strongest controlled baseline is modest and its uncertainty is insufficiently characterized. Table S2 reports edit accuracy of 5.94 versus 5.70, with slightly worse preservation and LPIPS. The human study covers only 45 image pairs and excludes cases where no method succeeded, without reporting the exclusion count or selection procedure. The 68% Wilson intervals do not establish robustness across tasks, repeated ratings, or training seeds.

Several ablation conclusions overstate the evidence. Contrary to a general performance drop from reducing the basis size, N=16 improves edit accuracy, CLIP direction, and preference against the rank-128 baseline. The composite encoder input also improves preference against that baseline from 57.9% to 61.9%, despite lowering standalone edit accuracy. These mixed outcomes do not clearly establish the claimed importance of a larger basis or the superiority of the default configuration.

Reference dependence is demonstrated only through selected examples. Quantitative reference-removal or reference-shuffling controls would better establish analogy understanding across the benchmark, especially because descriptive editing prompts are supplied. Figure 7 also omits the strongest same-backbone single-LoRA baseline.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: the manuscript claims code and data are available on a project website but supplies no identifiable URL. Targeted weight matrices, adapter scaling and initialization, inference settings, and the exact Gemma-3 checkpoint are not specified. Router parameter overhead and measured runtime or memory costs are also absent.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer-vision problem: transferring edits whose visual details are difficult to specify through text. Jointly learning LoRA factors and an image-conditioned router provides a practical adaptation mechanism without per-example optimization.

The evaluation includes a valuable same-backbone, approximately parameter-matched rank-128 LoRA baseline. LoRWeB achieves 57.9% VLM preference and 57.6% human preference against this baseline, providing evidence of a benefit beyond simply using FLUX.1-Kontext.

The qualitative examples demonstrate convincing transfer of styles, inserted objects, and appearance details. Figure 7 is particularly useful: changing the exemplar while retaining the prompt changes crown colors and poster details, supporting actual use of visual conditioning.

Experiments cover 100 tasks and 840 triplets, aggregate scores by task, and combine several automated metrics with human judgments. The appendix supplies optimization settings, encoder checkpoints, evaluation prompts, and attribution for image sources and community LoRAs.
weaknesses: The central mechanism is insufficiently isolated. The router introduces additional CLIP conditioning as well as dynamic weights, but there are no fixed-mixture, shuffled-routing, or comparable CLIP-conditioned single-adapter controls. Consequently, the experiments do not establish how much improvement comes specifically from composing transformation primitives. Related mixture-of-LoRA methods are acknowledged, but the algorithmic distinction from them receives limited analysis.

The weight-basis interpretation needs qualification. Equation (2) mixes A and B separately, producing an update sum over i,j of e_i e_j B_i A_j, rather than a linear combination of the individual updates B_i A_i. This is a valid parameterization, but introduces cross terms and retains rank at most r. The paper neither investigates these interactions nor compares against mixing complete LoRA updates, weakening its explanation of why the method works.

The strongest generalization claims exceed the evaluation breakdown provided. The custom exemplars are generated with Kontext or Kontext-specific LoRAs, and in-domain prompts are filtered for successful Kontext edits. This may favor the chosen backbone relative to FLUX.1-Dev competitors, although the same-backbone baseline partly addresses that concern. Results are pooled rather than separately reported for Relation252k, in-domain, and out-of-domain tasks, making the claimed improvement on genuinely difficult unseen transformations hard to assess.

The human evidence is encouraging but limited: 33 users evaluate only 45 image pairs, after cases where all methods fail are removed. Selection criteria and exclusion counts are unspecified. Figure 6 reports 68% Wilson intervals without explaining how repeated judgments and shared tasks are handled. Cluster-aware uncertainty and training-seed variability are particularly relevant to the modest preference margin over the strongest baseline.

Some empirical interpretations are stronger than the results support. Against rank-128 LoRA, edit accuracy rises from 5.70 to 5.94, while preservation falls from 7.99 to 7.87 and LPIPS worsens from 0.27 to 0.31: this is a useful tradeoff, not uniform superiority. Likewise, reducing the basis to 16 improves several metrics and preference rates in Table 1, so the stated importance of a larger basis is not consistently demonstrated.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful appendix: targeted weight matrices, adapter scaling and initialization, inference settings, exact Gemma-3 checkpoint, and baseline configurations are not sufficiently specified. Overall, under Algorithms/General, the promising practical results make this a close decision, but uncertainty about causal attribution and unseen-task generalization supports a borderline rejection.

strengths: The paper presents a useful Algorithms/General contribution: jointly learning LoRA factors and an image-conditioned router to produce task-specific adapters for visual analogy editing. The construction is straightforward and avoids per-example optimization at inference.

The matched-backbone, approximately capacity-matched comparison provides meaningful evidence beyond comparisons with older systems. Against a rank-128 LoRA on Flux.1-Kontext, LoRWeB obtains 57.6% human preference and 57.9% VLM preference. Table S2 also shows improved editing accuracy, albeit with slightly worse preservation.

Qualitative results demonstrate convincing transfer of reference-specific details. Figure 7 holds the prompt and target image fixed while changing the reference pair, showing changes in crown appearance and poster design that cannot be explained by the text prompt alone.

Evaluation combines 840 triplets across 100 tasks, several automated metrics, and human judgments. Ablations cover adapter capacity, routing normalization, encoder choice, and input layout. The appendix supplies training settings, evaluation prompts, and attribution for source images and community adapters.
weaknesses: The central mechanism is not fully isolated. A fixed or uniform mixture, a single rank-4 adapter, and a closely matched mixture-of-LoRA-experts baseline would help establish whether gains arise specifically from input-dependent composition. Moreover, Eq. (2) mixes factors separately: the resulting update contains cross terms between different adapters, rather than being a linear combination of their weight updates. The relationship between this construction and the claimed semantic basis needs clearer explanation and evidence.

The generalization benchmark has important scope limitations. Most evaluation tasks are custom transformations generated using Kontext or its community adapters, and in-domain prompts are filtered for successful Kontext edits. This favors a particular model ecosystem. Results are pooled across the released Relation252k tasks and the custom in-domain/out-of-domain subsets, making the claimed improvement on genuinely unseen transformations difficult to assess separately.

The human study covers only 45 image pairs and excludes cases where all methods fail, without reporting the exclusion rate or detailed allocation across baselines. The reported 68% Wilson intervals do not establish uncertainty across tasks and repeated judgments. This matters particularly for the modest advantage over the matched LoRA baseline. Appendix A.3 reports 66.7% human–VLM agreement; dividing this by human–human agreement does not establish near-human evaluator reliability.

Some ablation conclusions overstate the evidence. Table 1's N=16 model matches or exceeds the default on editing accuracy, CLIP direction, and several pairwise comparisons, while N=64 performs worse in Table S2. These results do not clearly establish that a larger basis improves generalization. Multiple training seeds and task-level uncertainty would help distinguish small differences.

Comparisons with the three published methods also change the backbone from Flux.1-Dev to Kontext, limiting architectural attribution. Reproducibility would benefit from exact adapted layers, factor initialization and scaling, inference settings, and measured parameter/runtime overhead. These concerns temper the broad state-of-the-art claim, although the matched-Kontext comparison supports a narrower positive conclusion.

strengths: Assessed as Algorithms/General, the paper presents a coherent, practically useful approach to visual analogy editing: jointly learned LoRA experts are composed through input-dependent, layer-specific routing. Combining semantic routing with direct image conditioning is well motivated, and the method avoids per-example optimization.

The same-backbone rank-128 LoRA comparison provides meaningful evidence beyond comparisons with older systems. LoRWeB improves VLM edit accuracy from 5.70 to 5.94 and achieves 57.9% VLM preference and 57.6% human preference against this baseline. These are modest but consistent improvements, obtained with only 3.1% measured inference overhead.

Evaluation covers 840 triplets across 100 tasks, multiple competing methods, human judgments, and ablations of expert count, rank, normalization, and image encoder. The supplementary higher-rank single-LoRA results help establish that simply increasing adapter capacity does not reproduce the benefit.

The qualitative examples show convincing transfer of reference-specific details, including crown colors and poster designs. Experiments with less descriptive prompts support the claim that reference images influence editing. The discussion candidly documents failures involving subtle edits, multiple transformation components, and mismatched reference pairs.
weaknesses: The architectural novelty relative to existing mixtures of LoRA experts is insufficiently distinguished. The paper cites these methods but provides little direct technical comparison. LoRA of Change [60], which generates editing LoRAs from before-and-after pairs, is particularly relevant but is not evaluated; the general statement that hypernetworks are difficult to train does not establish an advantage over this specific approach. The contribution is more convincingly supported as an effective visual-editing adaptation than as a fundamentally new weight-space framework.

The central generalization claim needs more granular evidence. Most evaluation tasks come from a custom set generated with Flux.1-Kontext or its community LoRAs, and in-domain prompts are filtered for successful Kontext edits. This favors compatibility with the proposed backbone, although the same-backbone LoRA comparison mitigates that concern. Results are not separated for the public test set, custom in-domain edits, and community-LoRA edits. Moreover, different prompt wording does not by itself establish a genuinely unseen transformation. The few non-Flux examples in Appendix B.6 cannot establish broad absence of generator bias.

The evidence for the specific routing mechanism remains incomplete. A single rank-128 LoRA is a valuable control, but there is no constant-routing, shuffled-routing, or router-input ablation to establish that analogy-dependent expert selection drives the gain. No expert-usage or specialization analysis supports the interpretation of learned transformation primitives. Table 1 also does not consistently support the stated importance of a larger basis: N=16 improves several reported metrics over N=32.

The human study is small at 45 image pairs and excludes cases where neither method succeeds, so its preference rates do not characterize the full evaluation distribution. Allocation of judgments across baselines and handling of repeated ratings are unclear. The reported 68% Wilson intervals and absence of training-seed variation leave uncertainty around the modest same-backbone gain. VLM order randomization is also unspecified. Appendix A.4's 66.7% human–VLM agreement divided by 74.2% human–human agreement should not be interpreted as 89.9% human-level evaluation reliability.

Several reproducibility and mathematical details require clarification. The exact adapted weight matrices, LoRA scaling and initialization, inference settings, and Gemma-3 checkpoint are not specified. Equation (2) mixes factors, whereas Equation (5) mixes their products; these are different operations and their relationship should be explicit. Equation (4) also has a transpose inconsistent with the stated dimensions of K. Finally, softmax mixing explores the convex hull of the learned updates, rather than spanning the entire space of rank-Nr adapters. These issues are mostly correctable, but the current language overstates the mathematical scope.

strengths: Assessed as Algorithms/General, LoRWeB offers a useful adaptation of jointly learned, input-conditioned LoRA mixtures to visual analogy editing. Layer-specific routing provides task-dependent model adaptation without per-example optimization, and the reported inference overhead is only 3.1% over a standard LoRA (Appendix A.2).

The paper includes a meaningful matched-backbone control: a rank-128 LoRA trained on Flux.1-Kontext. LoRWeB achieves 57.9% VLM preference and 57.6% human preference against this baseline. These results support a modest benefit beyond simply adopting a stronger backbone; the rank-256 comparison also helps address whether additional adapter capacity alone explains improvements.

Evaluation combines perceptual metrics, VLM judgments, human preferences, and extensive qualitative comparisons. Figures 7–8 provide useful evidence that reference images influence details beyond the textual instruction. The appendix adds comparisons with optimization-based methods and reports informative failure cases.

The manuscript supplies training settings, evaluation prompts, data sources, and community-adapter identifiers, and acknowledges practical limitations involving reference-pair alignment and unfamiliar transformations. Overall, the practical contribution and convergent empirical evidence support a slight preference for acceptance.
weaknesses: The central generalization claim is stronger than the benchmark establishes. Most evaluation tasks come from a custom set generated using Flux.1-Kontext or its community LoRAs, and the in-domain subset explicitly excludes prompts on which Kontext fails. Novel prompt wording does not itself establish novel transformation types. Separate quantitative results for the original held-out tasks, custom in-domain tasks, and community-LoRA tasks are needed; the few non-Flux examples in Appendix B.6 do not establish generator independence.

The methodological advance over existing mixture-of-LoRA approaches is insufficiently isolated. Such approaches are cited, but there is no controlled comparison with a simpler router, shared routing across layers, or input-independent learned mixture. Nor is there analysis showing that experts learn reusable transformation primitives. The proposed module may be effective, but the interpretation as a semantic basis remains largely hypothetical.

Improvements over the strongest controlled baseline are relatively small and involve tradeoffs. Table S3 reports edit accuracy increasing from 5.70 to 5.94, while preservation decreases from 7.99 to 7.87 and LPIPS worsens from 0.27 to 0.31. Larger gains against other methods partly involve a backbone difference: those methods use Flux.1-Dev. Repeated training runs and task-level uncertainty estimates would clarify the reliability of the matched-backbone improvement.

The human study covers only 45 image pairs and filters out cases where no method succeeded, without sufficiently specifying selection criteria, excluded counts, or per-comparison sample sizes. This limits interpretation of its preference rates. The 68% Wilson intervals do not address dependence among votes sharing images or participants. Appendix A.4's ratio of 66.7% human–VLM agreement to 74.2% human–human agreement should not be interpreted as establishing 89.9% human-equivalent evaluation reliability.

Some architectural claims and ablation conclusions need qualification. Softmax mixing restricts each layer's updates to the convex hull of its learned expert updates, rather than spanning the general space of rank-Nr matrices. Table 1 also provides mixed support for the claimed importance of a larger basis: N=16 matches or exceeds the default on several metrics. Exact adapted weight matrices, LoRA scaling and initialization, total trainable parameter counts including routers, and inference settings would improve reproducibility.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer-vision problem: transferring an edit from a reference image pair while preserving the target subject. Under Algorithms/General, the jointly learned LoRA bank and image-conditioned, layer-specific router constitute a coherent contribution with practical value.

The same-backbone rank-128 LoRA comparison provides meaningful evidence beyond comparisons against older systems. LoRWeB achieves 57.6% human preference and 57.9% VLM preference against this baseline, with larger preference margins against the other principal baselines (Fig. 6).

The approach avoids per-example optimization and adds little measured inference cost: 33.4 seconds versus 32.4 seconds for a conventional LoRA (Appendix A.2). This makes dynamic adaptation practically attractive.

Evaluation combines perceptual metrics, VLM judgments, human preferences, and qualitative comparisons. Reference-pair and reduced-prompt experiments provide useful evidence that the model transfers visual information beyond the textual instruction.

The supplementary material provides training settings, evaluation prompts, data-source attribution, additional baselines, and informative failure cases. The discussion candidly acknowledges difficulties with substantially novel transformations, subtle edits, and imperfectly aligned reference pairs.
weaknesses: The central generalization claim is only partially established. The custom benchmark supplies 90 of the 100 equally weighted tasks and uses references generated by Kontext or its community LoRAs; its in-domain portion additionally filters out prompts that Kontext cannot edit successfully. This favors the chosen backbone's visual distribution. Separate quantitative results for Relation252k, custom in-domain, and custom out-of-domain tasks are needed. The few non-Flux examples in Appendix B.6 do not establish absence of this bias, and differing prompt wording does not by itself establish semantic novelty relative to training.

The improvement over the strongest controlled baseline is modest and involves a tradeoff. Table S3 reports edit accuracy increasing from 5.70 to 5.94, but preservation decreasing from 7.99 to 7.87 and LPIPS increasing from 0.27 to 0.31. These results support a useful alternative operating point, rather than uniform superiority. No repeated-training results or task-level uncertainty estimates establish the stability of these differences.

The human study covers only 45 image pairs, despite collecting responses from 33 users, and excludes cases where no method successfully edits. The selection procedure and per-baseline sample counts are insufficiently specified. The reported 68% Wilson intervals do not explain how repeated judgments of the same images or shared raters are handled. Thus, the small preference margin over rank-128 LoRA warrants caution. Likewise, dividing 66.7% human–VLM agreement by 74.2% human–human agreement does not establish 89.9% evaluator reliability.

Originality is narrower than the framing suggests because input-conditioned mixtures of LoRA experts are already acknowledged in the related work. The paper would benefit from a sharper explanation of its distinction from these methods and direct evidence for the proposed basis interpretation. Constant or shuffled routing controls, routing-diversity analysis, and comparisons with a simpler conditional adapter would help isolate why the method works. Table 1 also gives mixed support for the claimed importance of a larger basis: N=16 matches or exceeds the default on several metrics.

Reproducibility and mathematical presentation need clarification. The manuscript does not fully specify adapted weight matrices, adapter initialization/scaling, inference sampling settings, the Gemma-3 checkpoint, or exact total trainable parameter counts including routers. Equation (2) mixes factors separately, whereas Equation (5) mixes their products; these are different operations and should be explicitly distinguished. These are addressable issues, but they complicate faithful implementation and assessment of the capacity comparison.
